stimulus.text:
| Power | Under the Articles of Confederation | Under the Constitution |
|---|---|---|
| Levy taxes on citizens | No — Congress could only ask the states for money | Yes |
| Regulate trade between the states | No | Yes |
| Raise an army | No — Congress could only ask the states for troops | Yes |
| Make treaties with other nations | Yes | Yes |
| Coin money | Yes | Yes |
| Change the frame of government | Only with the agreement of all thirteen states | With the agreement of three-fourths of the states |
stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the Articles of Confederation (1777-1781) and the Constitution of the United States (1787). Public domain documents.

books.section: Topic 3.7 The Articles of Confederation, B. The Articles of Confederation and the Critical Period

stem: The table best supports which conclusion about the government under the Articles of Confederation?

options.text: Congress could do nothing at all without the approval of the states
options.misconception: The table shows Congress could make treaties and coin money on its own.

options.text: Congress could act abroad but could not tax or raise an army
Congress could tax citizens but not regulate trade
options.misconception: The table says the opposite: Congress could not tax citizens under the Articles.

options.text: Congress held the same powers as under the Constitution
options.misconception: Four of the six rows change between the two columns.

rationales.B: The table gives Congress treaties and coinage under the Articles, but no power to levy taxes, regulate trade, or raise an army, so it could act abroad while remaining weak at home.
rationales.A: Congress could make treaties and coin money without asking the states.
rationales.C: The table says Congress could not levy taxes under the Articles.
rationales.D: The tax, trade, army, and amendment rows all change between the two columns.
rationales.general:
1. Sort the rows. Treaties and coinage stay Yes under the Articles.
2. Taxes, trade, and the army all read No under the Articles and Yes under the Constitution.
3. That split means a government that could act abroad but not at home.
4. Background: the split is the Articles in one picture, strong abroad and weak at home.
Remember: the Articles made Congress a diplomat, not a ruler.
